Redcar and Cleveland's population increased by around 1,400 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 140,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Redcar and Cleveland increased by 1.0%, from just under 135,200 in 2011 to around 136,500 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the North East (1.9%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Redcar and Cleveland was home to around 4.0 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 3.9 in 2011. This area was close to the median population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Redcar and Cleveland than across the North East

An older Redcar and Cleveland

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Redcar and Cleveland increased by three years, from 43 to 46 years of age.

This area had the second-highest average (median) age in the North East (behind Northumberland) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 2,800 (an increase of 10.3%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just over 4,700 (17.2% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.9 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Religion in Redcar and Cleveland

In 2021, 40.2% of Redcar and Cleveland residents reported having "No religion", up from 22.2% in 2011. The rise of 18.0 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Redcar and Cleveland. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 23.4% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 53.0% of people in Redcar and Cleveland described themselves as Christian (down from 70.4%), while 5.3% did not state their religion (down from 6.5% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 40.2% of usual residents in Redcar and Cleveland reported having "No religion"

Change in work hours

In 2021, 10.2% of Redcar and Cleveland residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked over 49 hours per week. This figure decreased from 10.9% in 2011.

This area had the region’s second highest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week. Across the region, only Sunderland, with 7.6%, had a lower percentage.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 0.7 percentage points

Unpaid care in Redcar and Cleveland

Redcar and Cleveland saw the North East's largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 7.0% in 2011 to 4.2% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Darlington saw the North East's next largest decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 7.0% in 2011 to 4.4% in 2021).

Every local authority area across the North East saw a fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion fell from 6.8% to 4.3%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 2.8 percentage points

Fewer couples with dependent children

Redcar and Cleveland saw the North East's joint second-largest percentage-point fall (alongside County Durham) in the proportion of households including a couple with dependent children (from 17.8% in 2011 to 15.7% in 2021).

Across the region, only Northumberland saw a greater fall in the percentage of households including a couple with dependent children (from 18.7% to 15.7%).

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 2.2 percentage points

Marriage and civil partnership in Redcar and Cleveland

Redcar and Cleveland saw the North East's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who were married (or in a civil partnership) (from 47.6% in 2011 to 44.0% in 2021).

Across the region, only County Durham saw a greater fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were married (or in a civil partnership) (from 47.4% to 43.4%).

Every local authority area across the North East saw a fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were married (or in a civil partnership), as the regional percentage fell from 45.7% to 43.0%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who were married or in a civil partnership in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 3.6 percentage points

Redcar and Cleveland residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 129,800 Redcar and Cleveland residents said they were born in England. This represented 95.1% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 129,100 in 2011, which at the time represented 95.5% of Redcar and Cleveland's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just under 1,900 Redcar and Cleveland residents reporting this country of birth (1.4%). This figure was down from around 2,200 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.6% of the population of Redcar and Cleveland.

The number of Redcar and Cleveland residents born in Germany rose from just under 450 in 2011 (0.3% of the local population) to just under 500 in 2021 (0.4%).

In 2021, 95.1% of Redcar and Cleveland residents reported their country of birth as England

Fall in unemployment

Redcar and Cleveland saw the North East's third-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were unemployed (from 5.9% in 2011 to 3.1% in 2021).

Across the region, only Hartlepool (from 7.0% to 3.5%) and Middlesbrough (from 6.9% to 3.8%) saw a greater decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were unemployed.

Every local authority area across the North East saw a fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were unemployed, as the regional percentage fell from 4.8% to 3.0%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 2.8 percentage points

Disability in Redcar and Cleveland

In 2021, 10.1% of Redcar and Cleveland residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 11.5% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just over one in nine people (11.3%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 11.2% in 2011. The proportion of Redcar and Cleveland residents who were not disabled increased from 77.3% to 78.6%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot was greater across the North East (1.8 percentage points, from 11.6% to 9.8%) than in Redcar and Cleveland (1.4 percentage points). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Redcar and Cleveland decreased by 1.4 percentage points

Health in Redcar and Cleveland

In 2021, 44.1% of Redcar and Cleveland residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 42.3% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.1% to 34.0%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Redcar and Cleveland residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.7% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 6.0% to 5.4%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Redcar and Cleveland increased by 1.8 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Of Redcar and Cleveland households, 15.8% rented privately in 2021, up from 12.5% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in five households (18.9%) lived in socially rented housing, compared with 19.4% in 2011. The percentage of Redcar and Cleveland households that owned their home (outright or with a mortgage or loan) decreased from 66.6% to 64.7%.

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes was greater across the North East (3.6 percentage points, from 13.7% to 17.2%) than in Redcar and Cleveland (3.3 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.6 percentage points, from 16.8% to 20.5%.

Private renting in Redcar and Cleveland increased by 3.3 percentage points

National identity in Redcar and Cleveland

In 2021, 1.5% of Redcar and Cleveland residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 0.9% in 2011.

In 2021, 0.4% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.2% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Redcar and Cleveland that identified as "British only" increased from 12.6% to 58.3%.

This area had the country's joint lowest percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK and the lowest percentage of people who identified with a UK and non-UK national identity (alongside South Staffordshire and Staffordshire Moorlands). Copeland had England's next-lowest percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK (1.6%), while City of London had the country's highest percentage (33.1%).

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Redcar and Cleveland increased by 0.5 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Redcar and Cleveland

In 2021, 0.4% of Redcar and Cleveland residents identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group"), up from 0.1% in 2011. The 0.3 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North East, the percentage of people from the "Other ethnic groups" ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.4% to 1.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 1.0% to 2.2%.

In 2021, 97.7% of people in Redcar and Cleveland identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 98.5% in 2011), while 0.9% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.6% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category increased from 0.6% in 2011 to 0.8% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
